items.title: [eff.org] US communities split over police license-plate cameras and privacy rules
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Communities across the United States are taking different approaches to police automated license-plate reader (ALPR) networks: voters in York, Maine, and League City, Texas, rejected their use, while Cedar Rapids approved a nearly $500,000 switch from Flock Safety to Axon without increasing its network of 70 cameras. Springfield, Massachusetts, has not advanced a proposed ban; councilors plan to review possible safeguards before deciding whether to send it forward. The systems record plates, timestamps and locations. Police say they can help investigate crimes and find missing people, while privacy advocates warn about tracking, misuse and data sharing beyond local jurisdictions. Suffolk County’s sheriff’s office has data-sharing relationships with slightly more than 400 agencies, established through system settings rather than formal written agreements. Ohio lawmakers are considering House Bill 725, which would set statewide rules for police use of plate data and make misuse a fifth-degree felony. The ACLU of Ohio argues the bill regulates data only after collection and could reduce public access to search information. Springfield’s committee plans to meet again after consulting the city’s Law Department.

items.title: [justinangel.net] Windows Phone 7 – Emulator Automation
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Hi Folks,

In this next blog post we’ll review how to automate the Windows Phone 7 Emulator and what are some real-world usages this technique.

This blog post is the second blog post in a series of unrelated advanced Windows Phone 7 blog posts.
The previous blog post in this series is “Windows Phone 7 – Unlocked ROMs”.

 

Why is Windows Phone 7 Automation Important?

Currently, the Windows Phone 7 Emulator can only launch developer packages (XAPs) from inside Visual Studio 2010.
Meaning, if we’ve got a XAP we can’t get the emulator to load it without Visual Studio.

As we’ve seen in a previous blog post the emulator can be launched and even installed on machines that do not have Visual Studio. More on that here.
Let’s consider that in order to load XAPs into the Emulator we currently have to use Visual Studio. 

The problem is – How do we load XAPs into WP7 Emulators and Devices without using Visual Studio?

So how does our Build Server run nightly tests? Or how do our customers see our applications?

Customers and Build servers don't have Visual Studio 2010 installed.

So, how can we deploy XAPs to an emulator running on these machines?

 

Quit your Jibber-Jabber, show me how to automate the WP7 emulator!

Let’s create a new solution with a Console Application and a Windows Phone 7 Project.

We’ll use the ConsoleApplication as our automation harness that can run on any computer with the .Net framework.
The WindowsPhone Application is the application whose deployment we’ll automate.

 

The CoreCon 10 WP7 API

The secret sauce for WP7 Automation is the CoreCon API.
These CoreCon DLLs have been in deep hibernation since 2007 when they last got a major upgrade.
For WP7 Tools the CoreCon API has been updated and are used by Visual Studio 2010 when deploying applications to WP7 devices and emulators.

Let’s add a reference to Microsoft.SmartDevice.Connectivity.dll from the CoreCon API.
On a x64 developer box, the DLL can be found at: C:\Program Files (x86)\Common Files\microsoft shared\Phone Tools\CoreCon\10.0\Bin\Microsoft.Smartdevice.Connectivity.dll 

 

 

Now that we have the CoreCon DLL reference in place, we can start automating WP7.

Here’s the User Experience we’re aiming for in this demo:

We’ll have to build the following workflow:

     

We’ll start off by getting an instance of the WP7 CoreCon SDK instance to work with:

// Get CoreCon WP7 SDK

DatastoreManager dsmgrObj = new DatastoreManager(1033);

 

Platform WP7SDK = dsmgrObj.GetPlatforms().Single(p => p.Name == "New Windows Mobile 7 SDK");

 

Next up we’ll have to get a reference to either a WP7 physical device or a WP7 Emulator.
This demo will use the emulator, but if we set “useEmulator = false” this demo will try and connect to a physical WP7 device.

// Get Emulator / Device

bool useEmulator = true;

Device WP7Device = null;

if (useEmulator)

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Emulator");

else

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Device");

Now we’ll launch the WP7 Emulator/Device.
Note that the default WP7 Emulator Image is the one we’ll launch into, and in a previous blog post I’ve explained how to use the Unlocked ROM as the default ROM.

// Connect to WP7 Emulator / Device

Console.WriteLine("Connecting to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

WP7Device.Connect();

Console.WriteLine("Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device Connected...");

Next, we’ll have to check if our application is already installed, and if it is – we’ll uninstall it.
Since the the UpdateApplication Method in the current CoreCon API doesn’t work, this is our best bet on easily updating installed apps.

In order to Install or Uninstall our application, we’ll need it’s Application Product Identifier (GUID).
We can get the application GUID from the Properties/WMAppManifest.xml file.

 

We’ll write the code to check if an application is installed, and if it is – we’ll uninstall it.

Guid appID = new Guid("{5e75bba1-fbf6-463c-94ac-fa4a78f8fd12}");

RemoteApplication app;

if (WP7Device.IsApplicationInstalled(appID))

{

    Console.WriteLine("Uninstalling sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

    app = WP7Device.GetApplication(appID);

    app.Uninstall();

 

    Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP Uninstalled from Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

}

At this point, we’ll install our XAP.
In order to do that, we’ll need 3 pieces of information:
1. The location of our XAP.
2. The Application GUID.
3. The location of the application icon.

// Install XAP

Console.WriteLine("Installing sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

app = WP7Device.InstallApplication(

    appID,

    appID,

    "NormalApp",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\ApplicationIcon.png",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\Bin\Debug\WindowsPhoneApplication1.xap");

 

Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP installed to Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

The last step is to actually launch our application.

// Launch Application

Console.WriteLine("Launching sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

app.Launch();

Console.WriteLine("Launched sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

 

We’re done. And indeed when we run our sample application the app runs as expected:

 

So What is WP7 Automation good for?

There’s a lot of good use cases: Automating Unit tests, Loading Nightly builds into the emulator and even letting customers use the WP7 Emulator.
There’s really a plethora of reasons and situations WP7 Automation can prove useful in and it’s up to you to figure it out for your projects.

For instance in Vertigo, we’re using the WP7 Automation harness to run the WP7 Emulator on multi-touch laptops that our customers have.
So Vertigo’s customers, as part of an iterative process, get access to our current build without having to install or use Visual Studio 2010.

 

Access to Isolated Storage

One use-case in particular interests me, which is automating running all unit tests in the project after a Continuous Integration nightly build.

We can pretty much do all of the work to automate WP7 tests using WP7 Automation we’ve seen so far, but how do we get results into application? Or get instructions in?

The easiest method I can think off is communicate through cold storage – read & write files into Isolated Storage.

We’ll start off by writing a file into our WP7 Application IsoStore.
Remember that this code executes in the WP7 Emulator/Device.

public MainPage()

{

    InitializeComponent();

 

    SupportedOrientations = SupportedPageOrientation.Portrait | SupportedPageOrientation.Landscape;

 

    using (var isoStore = IsolatedStorageFile.GetUserStoreForApplication())

    using (var sw = new StreamWriter(isoStore.OpenFile("Foo.txt", FileMode.OpenOrCreate, FileAccess.Write)))

    {

        sw.Write("Hello WP7! (Written from WP7 IsoStore, read by Console Harness!)");

    }

}

Basically, We’ve written a Foo.txt file into our IsoStore and added some text into it.

Next, we would have used the RemoteIsolatedStorage class and get access to the emulator IsoStore, but that has not been enabled yet in CoreCon10.

We would have used RemoteApplication.GetIsolatedStorage() but that has not been implemented yet.

We’ll use a FileDeployer class instead.
There’s some reflection magic associated with getting a copy of a FileDeployer class that can be used for our application.

Thread.Sleep(10000);

//app.GetIsolatedStore(); <-- Throws NotImplementedException

object ConManServer = WP7Device.GetType().GetField("mConmanServer", BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance).GetValue(WP7Device);

FileDeployer f = (FileDeployer)typeof(FileDeployer).GetConstructors(BindingFlags.Instance | BindingFlags.NonPublic)[0].Invoke(new object[] { ConManServer });

Next, we’ll copy the Foo.txt file from the application isolated storage into our local binary folder and read it into the console:

f.ReceiveFile(@"\Applications\Data\" + appID + @"\data\isolatedstore\Foo.txt", @"\Foo.txt");

 

Console.WriteLine("\t" + File.ReadAllText(@"foo.txt"));

 

When we run this sample we can see the text written from IsoStore showing up on our console.

And we’re done, we’ve esteblished a two-way communication channel between WP7 Emulator/Device and Managed .net code.  

 

Console WP7 Automation Harness Source Code

Here’s the source code we’ve built in this project:

// Get CoreCon WP7 SDK

DatastoreManager dsmgrObj = new DatastoreManager(1033);

 

Platform WP7SDK = dsmgrObj.GetPlatforms().Single(p => p.Name == "New Windows Mobile 7 SDK");

 

// Get Emulator / Device

bool useEmulator = true;

Device WP7Device = null;

if (useEmulator)

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Emulator");

else

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Device");

 

// Connect to WP7 Emulator / Device

Console.WriteLine("Connecting to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

WP7Device.Connect();

Console.WriteLine("Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device Connected...");

 

 

Guid appID = new Guid("{5e75bba1-fbf6-463c-94ac-fa4a78f8fd12}");

RemoteApplication app;

if (WP7Device.IsApplicationInstalled(appID))

{

    Console.WriteLine("Uninstalling sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

    app = WP7Device.GetApplication(appID);

    app.Uninstall();

 

    Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP Uninstalled from Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

}

 

// Install XAP

Console.WriteLine("Installing sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

app = WP7Device.InstallApplication(

    appID,

    appID,

    "NormalApp",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\ApplicationIcon.png",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\Bin\Debug\WindowsPhoneApplication1.xap");

 

Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP installed to Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

 

// Launch Application

Console.WriteLine("Launching sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

app.Launch();

Console.WriteLine("Launched sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

 

Console.WriteLine("Reading Foo.txt Isolated Storage file:");

 

Thread.Sleep(10000);

//app.GetIsolatedStore(); <-- Throws NotImplementedException

object ConManServer = WP7Device.GetType().GetField("mConmanServer", BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance).GetValue(WP7Device);

FileDeployer f = (FileDeployer)typeof(FileDeployer).GetConstructors(BindingFlags.Instance | BindingFlags.NonPublic)[0].Invoke(new object[] { ConManServer });

f.ReceiveFile(@"\Applications\Data\" + appID + @"\data\isolatedstore\Foo.txt", @"\Foo.txt");

 

Console.WriteLine("\t" + File.ReadAllText(@"foo.txt"));

 

Console.ReadLine();

 

Fin

In this blog post we’ve talked about why Automating the WP7 Emulator and Device deployment process is important and how to go about doing that.
Hopefully now you know how to automate WP7 XAP Deployment.

In the next blog post in this series we’ll talk about setting up a Continuous Integration build for WP7.

Sincerely,

-- Justin Angel

European carmakers are losing ground in their home market as hybrid demand grows. German manufacturers’ European Union sales fell 5.7% in October, and their market share dropped from 41.5% to 38.2%, according to figures cited by DW. On Nov. 24, the European Commission published temporary import quotas for hybrids from China and other exporters after its investigation found an imminent threat of serious injury to EU producers. The limits cover imports from major suppliers including Japan, Turkey, South Korea and the United Kingdom. The Commission said the restrictions are tightest for China, while most other countries’ allocations exceed recent shipments. German automakers have announced widespread layoffs as their market shares shrink. The Commission has linked import growth to global production overcapacity and trade barriers in other markets. The provisional measures run for up to 200 days, through June 18, 2027, while the Commission continues its investigation. Any longer-term measures would require backing from EU member states.

The group also called for a coordinated EU approach to high energy and diesel prices, arguing that differing national support measures could distort competition between farmers. It wants better rural grid connections, simpler permits and greater access to financing to help farms produce renewable energy. It also supports greater use of sustainably produced European biofuels to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.

Hackers breached an unclassified open-source intelligence analysis network used by the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), exposing some information, according to people familiar with the incident. A source told The Associated Press that the breach had been resolved and involved no classified information. Investigators have not identified the attacker or specified which records were exposed. Reports also indicated that the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was affected and that information at other government agencies may have been exposed. Access to analysts’ activity could reveal what U.S. intelligence agencies are tracking, even without access to classified files. Nextgov reported that investigators believe hackers used ARTEX, an AI-enabled intrusion tool, but U.S. officials have not publicly attributed the breach to a person, group or government.

items.content_html:

A suspected China-linked espionage group exploited a critical VMware vCenter authentication bypass from early September until Broadcom issued a patch on Nov. 19, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said. The flaw, CVE-2026-123890, lets an attacker with network access bypass sign-in and gain administrator access; it carries a severity score of 9.8 out of 10. Investigators traced the intrusion to an earlier breach of BeyondTrust Remote Support, after which attackers moved through internal Linux systems into vCenter and ESXi infrastructure. They found attackers using custom tools to create an administrator account, steal authentication material and access files inside virtual machines, including Windows Active Directory data. Google said it had confirmed compromises at a small number of organizations, with more likely affected. Broadcom classifies the update as an emergency change and lists no workaround.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] IEA says Iran shock speeds electrification but may prolong coal use
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The International Energy Agency says the energy disruption linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran is accelerating countries’ shift toward electrification. The agency said 25 countries had announced new electrification-related policies since February as governments seek more domestic energy sources. At the U.N. climate talks, COP31, host Türkiye is pressing to raise electricity’s share of global energy use from about 21% to 35% by 2035; draft negotiating text does not specify that the added power must come from renewables. The IEA also said buildings now use more energy for cooling than for heating, a shift it links to rising temperatures and demand for air conditioning. The agency expects solar and nuclear power to gain ground, but energy-security concerns could keep coal in use as backup, particularly in coal-rich Asian economies. It warned that inadequate electricity grids, charging infrastructure and supply capacity could slow electrification.

The alerts cover coastal areas from Metro Vancouver and Vancouver Island to Haida Gwaii and the central and Sunshine coasts. Victoria closed sections of its Dallas Road waterfront seawall, and Ucluelet closed beaches and trails. A new round of U.S. tariffs could add 2% to 7.5% to import duties if the administration uses the new levies to restore rates imposed before the Supreme Court struck them down, trade-policy expert Deborah Elms estimated. President Donald Trump’s administration is preparing country-specific duties on China, the European Union and 14 other economies following an investigation into industrial subsidies by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR); final rates and effective dates remain unsettled. The duties would focus largely on manufactured goods and could raise costs for importers and consumers. The July tariffs tied to forced-labor enforcement have already contributed to higher U.S. consumer-goods prices, the Associated Press reported. The administration is expected to keep overall tariff rates within ceilings set by existing trade deals rather than apply a single blanket rate. The European Union, Japan and South Korea face ceilings of 15% or less, while China’s ceiling is expected to remain at 20% if its trade truce with Washington is extended. The USTR is expected to release its findings shortly. Targeted economies can then seek changes through hearings, public comments and talks before rates are finalized. The administration could also reduce duties if countries take steps to address excess production capacity; the exact product list and start date remain unclear.

items.title: [bloomberg.com] Higher energy costs squeeze Chinese factories as household demand stays weak
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Chinese manufacturers are absorbing higher energy and raw-material costs while weak household spending limits their ability to raise prices. The National Bureau of Statistics said Monday that factory-gate prices rose 5.7% year over year in October, the fastest increase since June 2022, while consumer inflation slowed to 0.7%. Producer purchasing prices rose 7.9%, outpacing factory-gate prices, while output prices for consumer goods continued a decline lasting more than three years. Economists link weak demand to the prolonged property downturn, which has weighed on household confidence; exports helped lift third-quarter growth. China had experienced more than three years of producer-price deflation before the energy shock linked to the conflict in the Middle East pushed prices higher. Nguyen Hoang Nam, China economist at Capital Economics, expects the shock to persist for months before fading next year. He forecasts a return to producer-price deflation and average consumer inflation of 0.4% in 2027.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, flipping Senate seats in states including Texas, Ohio, Kansas and South Carolina. With 228 House seats and 54 Senate seats reported for the party, Democrats will control committees and confirmation votes when the new Congress convenes in January. President Donald Trump retains the power to veto legislation and direct executive policy. Voters’ concerns about living costs, inflation, tariffs and the Iran war contributed to Republican losses. items.content_html:

Chile’s Vera C. Rubin Observatory is conducting a decade-long survey that could help astronomers test whether distant icy bodies follow orbital patterns predicted for a hypothetical planet beyond Neptune. Its expanding catalogue will provide more objects to compare, but detecting the planet itself would be much harder because it would appear extremely faint. An international team led by Patryk Sofia Lykawka, a researcher at Japan’s Kindai University, used simulations of 4.5 billion years of Solar System evolution to propose Planet X2 as a possible explanation for some distant objects’ unusual orbits. Astronomers have not observed the planet, and the model does not match every feature of the known objects’ orbital distribution.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Federal memo warns freshwater pressures threaten Canada’s long-term security
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

items.title: [news.mit.edu] Older adults show weaker brain-clearing fluid waves during sleep
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

MIT researchers found that older adults had significantly weaker waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which helps clear waste from the brain during sleep, than younger adults. The researchers used brain imaging and electroencephalography to study volunteers ages 18 to 39 and 60 to 84, linking the reduced flow partly to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and diminished vascular responses. Separately, a study described in a paper shared on Reddit found that LSD-related gene-expression patterns in rats and mice ran counter to some patterns associated with human brain aging. LSD also reduced certain amyloid-beta-related changes in mouse brain-cell cultures. These are preclinical findings, not evidence that LSD prevents dementia in people.
